clue.text: Ageing criminal getting bird

parts.note: hair goes grey with age, so grey stands for ageing
an old lag is a habitual convict

explanation.surface: An elderly crook takes up birdwatching, or perhaps picks up a jail term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is also British slang for a prison sentence, which suits the criminal in the surface; here it is the plain feathered sense. LAG is British slang for a convict.
explanation.definitionFit: The greylag is a large grey wild goose of Europe, the ancestor of most farmyard geese.

clue.text: DS eager for excitement got moving with gun?

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters get thrown into a new order

parts.note: the letters of an abbreviation plus a word, all used as raw material

explanation.surface: A keen detective sergeant pulls out a firearm and charges off in search of thrills.
explanation.walkthrough: DS (Detective Sergeant) and the 'gun' both belong to a police story, but the gun is a grease gun, used to lubricate machinery so parts start moving freely.
explanation.definitionFit: Machinery lubricated from a grease gun runs freely, so something greased has been freed up to turn.

clue.text: Sentry regularly protecting MP — dead man?

indicators.note: a guard protecting someone stands all round them, so the selected letters surround the politician
at regular intervals, so every second letter of the guard's word is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the guard's title
used as it stands: Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A guard standing over a politician finds the MP is a corpse.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'dead man' is slang for an empty bottle, one that has been drunk dry; the question mark flags the slang sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinkers call a finished bottle a dead man, so a bottle with nothing left inside fits the slang phrase.

clue.text: Start to skip a meal

indicators.note: skipping something means leaving it out, so the word for start drops the article

parts.note: to start something off is to launch it
the article taken literally, as the letter to drop

explanation.surface: Advice to begin a diet by missing a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skip a meal' reads as one phrase, but 'to skip a' is the instruction: the word for start leaves out its A.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunch is the midday meal, one particular example of the general word.

clue.text: Setter's coming into favour? Look disgusted

indicators.note: entering something puts you inside it, so the setter's contraction goes inside the word for favour

parts.note: being in someone's good graces is being in their favour
the setter speaks of themself: the setter is = I am, contracted

explanation.surface: A setter gains approval, and someone looks on in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is the crossword's author, so 'setter's' means 'I'm', which goes inside the word for favour.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a twisted facial expression of distaste, and as a verb it means pulling such a face.

clue.text: Problems are back for Dutch scholar

indicators.note: reading something back means reading it from its end to its start

parts.note: arithmetic problems set as exercises
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A Dutch academic finds his troubles returning.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are written together and then read backwards as a single string.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the great Renaissance humanist and theologian from the Low Countries.

clue.text: First Lady needs doze: struggle getting up here?

parts.note: the first woman in Genesis
a doze is a short rest

explanation.surface: A president's wife, needing a nap, finds it hard to get out of bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First Lady' suggests a president's wife but means the first woman of all. The definition is cryptic: 'getting up' means climbing, not rising from bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The world's highest mountain is notoriously a hard climb, so it is a place where ascent is a struggle.

clue.text: Animal limb — bad trouble bandaging that?

parts.note: an arm is a limb

indicators.note: a bandage wraps round a wound, so the word for trouble is wound around the word for bad that precedes it

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble
ill means bad, as in ill will

explanation.surface: An injured limb causes trouble and needs a bandage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' comes before the container word but is what gets wrapped; 'that' points back to it, so the word for trouble wraps round the word for bad.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo is an armoured burrowing mammal of the Americas, a specific example of an animal.

clue.text: Sage old woman, stern one embracing upright character

indicators.note: an embrace puts arms around someone, so the stern word holds the upright letter within it

parts.note: one's old woman, informally, is one's mother
stern and severe
the letter that stands straight up
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A wise old woman who is stern but hugs a person of upright morals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright character' reads as a person of integrity, but it is the letter I, drawn as a single vertical stroke; it goes inside 'stern one'.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharishi is a Hindu holy teacher, literally a great seer, so a wise person or sage.

clue.text: Meet e.g. enthralling female model twirling

indicators.note: to enthral once meant to hold captive, so the word for e.g. holds the spun pair inside

parts.note: e.g. and say both introduce an example
standard abbreviation for female

indicators.note: twirling spins something round to face the other way, so the female and model pair turns back to front

parts.note: an artist's model sits for a portrait

explanation.surface: A fashion show where a woman spins on the catwalk and captivates the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model twirling' looks like a catwalk turn; the letters for female and model are joined, spun round, and held inside the word for e.g.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet demands or requirements is to fulfil them, the same as satisfying them.

clue.text: Dear European, cross and brooding

parts.note: standard abbreviation for European
a cross is shaped like the letter X
lost in gloomy thought

explanation.surface: Opening of a letter to a bad-tempered, moody continental friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' looks like a letter's greeting, and 'cross' like anger, but dear here means costly and cross is the letter shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dear costs a lot of money, the British sense of the word meaning high-priced.

clue.text: Yours truly might tip this rubbish!

definitions.meaning: 'yours truly' is the speaker, who might raise their headgear in greeting

explanation.surface: A letter-writer's sign-off turns into a scornful exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yours truly' means 'I, the speaker', so the object is one's own headgear. The second sense is a dated British exclamation, like 'my foot!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'my hat!' expresses scornful disbelief, the same force as calling a claim nonsense.

clue.text: City has fallen in ancient region

indicators.note: a fallen city lies in ruins, its parts tumbled out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: seven letters of raw material

explanation.surface: A city of the ancient world has been overrun.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a city conquered in antiquity; 'fallen' is the instruction to rearrange the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Scythia was the classical name for the steppe lands north of the Black Sea, home of nomadic horsemen.

clue.text: Bears are abandoning area in shifting dunes

indicators.note: abandoning something means leaving it behind, so the verb drops the letter for area
placing one thing in another puts the shortened verb inside the rearranged sand hills
shifting sands move and change shape, so the dunes' letters change their order

parts.note: raw material to be rearranged
the verb loses its A, the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Bears leave a region of drifting sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animals leaving, but it is a verb meaning puts up with.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear hardship is to tolerate or withstand it, so bears and endures are verb synonyms.

clue.text: Corrupt beauty by love retreat

parts.note: an attractive person is informally a dish
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
a snug hideaway

explanation.surface: A crooked beauty ruins a romantic getaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' simply sets the pieces side by side. 'Corrupt' could be a verb, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A corrupt official is one who lacks honesty and takes bribes, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Offer up pouch, with grain getting provided inside

parts.note: a sac is a bag or pouch in anatomy

indicators.note: the grain is getting, that is receiving, the conditional word into itself
inside says where the conditional word goes: within the grain rather than beside it

parts.note: a cereal grain
provided that means on condition, so if

explanation.surface: An offering of a bag of grain at a temple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Provided' looks like part of the surface, meaning supplied, but it is the conjunction meaning if.
explanation.definitionFit: To sacrifice is to offer something up to a god, or to give it away for a higher purpose.

clue.text: Amusing oneself at municipal expense?

parts.note: the surface reading: someone out enjoying themselves, perhaps nightclubbing
the setter's reading: the council is paying, so the bill falls on the local authority

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for a night out is read literally, as if the town were footing the bill, just as 'on the house' means free.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out enjoying the nightlife is the idiom's real meaning, while the clue plays on paid-for-by-the-council.

clue.text: Hearty, occasionally loud hovel

indicators.note: only now and then, so just every other letter of the noisy word is heard

parts.note: every other letter, starting with the first
a pigsty, or any filthy dwelling

explanation.surface: A cheerful shack where things sometimes get rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' takes alternate letters of the word that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lusty means vigorous and full of energy, as does hearty in a hearty appetite or lusty singing.

clue.text: Silent songbird catching a cold

indicators.note: catching something takes hold of it, so the bird's name closes around the article and the cold letter

parts.note: the tit is a small songbird
used as it stands
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A little bird goes quiet after catching a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catching a cold' reads as falling ill, but the bird is holding two letters inside itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means unspoken or implied without words, as in tacit consent, so it fits silent.

clue.text: Syrup in cereal stirred below temperature

indicators.note: in a down clue, below means lower in the column, so the jumbled cereal comes after the temperature letter

parts.note: standard abbreviation for temperature

indicators.note: stirring mixes a bowl of cereal about, so its letters get jumbled

parts.note: raw material to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Pouring syrup onto breakfast cereal and stirring it in before it cools.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'below' puts the rearranged cereal underneath the T. Treacle is the British word for dark syrup, close to molasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacle is a thick sweet syrup made in sugar refining, so it is a kind of syrup.

clue.text: Lecture from Emerson is garbled

indicators.note: garbled speech is muddled and confused, so the letters of the name and verb are scrambled

parts.note: the essayist's name plus a verb as raw material

explanation.surface: A talk by the American essayist Ralph Waldo Emerson came out muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lecture' looks like a noun, a talk given by Emerson, but it is the verb, to preach at someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To sermonise is to moralise at length like a preacher, which is to lecture someone.

clue.text: Literary family don't stand properly?

parts.note: the opposite of standing
done well is done properly

explanation.surface: A bookish family who slouch and never stand up straight.
explanation.walkthrough: Edith, Osbert and Sacheverell Sitwell were a trio of English writer siblings of the early twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sitwells were three English sibling writers famous together as a literary family.

clue.text: Ultimately thought man right to return ticket

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the string of pieces runs backwards
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the next word counts

parts.note: the final letter of the word
a chess man is a piece
standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A man decides to return his ticket after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but in chess or draughts the playing pieces are called men.
explanation.definitionFit: A receipt is a slip proving purchase, like a cloakroom or till ticket handed over after paying.

clue.text: Pain hard in each contest

parts.note: standard abbreviation for each, as on price lists

indicators.note: the letter for hard is placed in the word for contest, sitting within it

parts.note: a race is a contest of speed
H for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Every competition is a real hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter for hard sits inside the contest, near the end; the abbreviation for each simply comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is an ache in the ear, one specific kind of bodily pain.

clue.text: Papers in competition — that's obvious

indicators.note: papers entered in a competition sit within it, so the documents go inside the contest word

parts.note: a sporting event is a competition
identity papers, ID for short

explanation.surface: Someone entering documents into a contest, and the result is plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' suggests newspapers or essays, but it means identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evident is plain to see and clearly apparent, the same as obvious.

clue.text: Party worker Charlie dined on river

parts.note: C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
past tense of eat
re means on or about, as in a memo
standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A political activist named Charlie had dinner beside the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party worker' suggests a political party activist; here it means someone who serves food at a celebration. 'On' is not a link but the word RE, concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: A caterer supplies and serves food and drink at functions, so works at parties.

clue.text: Put a watch on?

parts.note: the surface reading: strapped a wristwatch on, or set a guard over someone
the setter's reading: held a stopwatch against a runner or event

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as fastening a timepiece to a wrist or posting surveillance; the answer is what a coach does with a stopwatch.
explanation.definitionFit: To measure how long something takes with a stopwatch is to clock it, a literal reading of the phrase.

clue.text: Proportion in harangue avoiding extremes

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, and avoiding them keeps only the middle

parts.note: a long speech is an oration; drop its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A moderate speaker urges balance and no extremism in a rant.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for a harangue must be found first, then trimmed at both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio expresses the relative size of two quantities, which is what a proportion describes.

clue.text: CO devouring breathable gases in city

indicators.note: devouring swallows something whole, so the commanding officer's letters engulf the gases

parts.note: used as it stands: commanding officer
the mixture of gases we breathe

explanation.surface: A commanding officer gulping down fresh air in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: CO also suggests carbon monoxide, a gas, which fits the 'gases' in the surface; here it is just two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairo is the capital of Egypt, one particular city on the Nile.

clue.text: Anagram etc aiming for cryptic

indicators.note: the setter simply names the device, telling the solver to rearrange the words that follow

parts.note: nine letters of raw material

explanation.surface: A setter's note about aiming anagrams and the like at a cryptic puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter names the device outright: the word 'Anagram' is itself the instruction to rearrange what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cryptic is mysterious and puzzling, with hidden meaning, which is what enigmatic means.

clue.text: Endless ale drunk: wind reportedly trapped

indicators.note: trapped wind is held inside, so the soundalike word is held within the jumbled beer
a drunk person staggers about, so the beer's letters stagger out of order

parts.note: raw material to be rearranged

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard or said, so we want a word pronounced like the synonym for wind

parts.note: to wind is to turn, and the seabird's name is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: Beer that flows forever leaves the drinker bloated with trapped wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as gas but is the verb, pronounced with a long I, meaning to twist or turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal means lasting forever without any end, the same as endless.

clue.text: This ultimately destined to leap when developed?

definitions.text: This ultimately destined to leap when developed?

indicators.note: developing changes something's form, as a larva's body changes, so the letters take a new shape
ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter of destined is used

parts.note: the last letter of the word
raw material to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A creature whose destiny, once it grows up, is to jump.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a larva that will one day hop as a frog, built from the letters of its own description.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is the larval stage of a frog, which on maturing becomes an animal that jumps.
